title: The Satellite Link
theme: Ship images over a tiny, unreliable link

missions.title: A Depot on the Ice
missions.story:
A yellow sticky note is taped to the server rack, in Ingrid Halvorsen's square handwriting:

"Satellite link: eleven minutes a day, billed by the megabyte. Every image we pull from the mainland gets paid for once, never twice. We need a depot here on the ice so that what we have already paid for stays on the station. It must survive a reboot, so keep its data on a named volume. - I.H."

Stand the depot up on port 5000.
objectives: Run a detached container named `depot` from `registry:2`
Publish host port `5000` to container port `5000`
Keep the registry's data in the named volume `depot-data`, mounted at `/var/lib/registry`
missions.startingState: A clean engine. The `registry:2` image is already on the machine.
hints: A registry is just another container: the official `registry:2` image speaks the same API as Docker Hub. You need a detached run, a published port, and somewhere durable for its data.

The registry stores everything under `/var/lib/registry`. Mount a named volume there with `-v NAME:/var/lib/registry`, publish the port with `-p 5000:5000`, and give the container the name `depot` with `--name`.

```bash
docker run -d --name depot \
  -p 5000:5000 \
  -v depot-data:/var/lib/registry \
  registry:2

curl http://localhost:5000/v2/
```

validation.description: Container `depot` is running from `registry:2`
Volume `depot-data` is mounted at `/var/lib/registry` in `depot`
Host port 5000 is published to container port 5000 of `depot`
The registry answers on http://localhost:5000/v2/

missions.debrief: A registry stores image layers in one directory, so a volume under `/var/lib/registry` is all it takes to make the depot outlive its container. Pro tip: `curl http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog` lists everything the depot holds.

missions.title: First Shipment
missions.story:
NORA: `OUTBOUND QUEUE: 0 IMAGES. DEPOT: ONLINE. kestrel/beacon:1.0: LOCAL ONLY.`

The depot is up on port 5000, but the beacon image Amara built exists only on this one machine's disk. If the disk goes, the image goes with it, and Ingrid wants every instrument host to fetch its images from the depot instead.

Publish `kestrel/beacon:1.0` to the depot, under the registry's own address, so anyone on the station can pull it.
objectives: The depot's catalog lists the repository `kestrel/beacon` with the tag `1.0`
missions.startingState: The `depot` registry is running on port 5000 and the image `kestrel/beacon:1.0` is built locally. The depot is empty.
hints: Docker decides where to push by reading the registry host out of the image name. An image called `kestrel/beacon` means Docker Hub; to reach the depot, the same image needs a second name that starts with the registry's address.
Add the name with `docker tag SOURCE TARGET`, where TARGET is `HOST:PORT/repo/name:tag`. Then `docker push TARGET`. You can read back what the depot holds at `http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog`.

```bash
docker tag kestrel/beacon:1.0 localhost:5000/kestrel/beacon:1.0
docker push localhost:5000/kestrel/beacon:1.0

curl http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/beacon/tags/list
```

files.content:
FROM nginx:alpine
LABEL station=kestrel role=beacon
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

validation.description: The image is tagged `localhost:5000/kestrel/beacon:1.0`
The depot's catalog lists `kestrel/beacon`
The depot has the tag `1.0` for `kestrel/beacon`
The manifest for `kestrel/beacon:1.0` can be fetched from the depot

missions.debrief: The registry host is part of an image's name, so pushing somewhere new always starts with `docker tag`. Pro tip: a tag is only a pointer, so tagging costs nothing and the push uploads each layer once.

missions.title: Round Trip
missions.story:
Station chat, 06:40.

**Tomasz:** The core-index image went up to the depot last night, and then Amara wiped the build machine. Before I stake the winter's index on that copy I need to know it is intact.

**Tomasz:** Pull it back from the depot. Then write its digest into `/workspace/digest.txt`, the sha256 exactly as the registry reports it, so I can compare it against my logbook. Precision, please.
objectives: Write the image's `sha256:...` digest into `/workspace/digest.txt`, matching what the depot reports
missions.startingState: The depot holds `kestrel/core-index:1.0`, but no copy of it is on this machine any more.
hints: An image you have pushed lives on in the registry even when your local copy is gone. Pulling brings it back, and a digest is the content hash that proves it is the same bytes.

Pull with the full registry name. Afterwards `docker images --digests` shows the digest column, and `docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'` prints `name@sha256:...`. Only the part starting at `sha256:` belongs in the file.

```bash
docker pull localhost:5000/kestrel/core-index:1.0
docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' \
  localhost:5000/kestrel/core-index:1.0 | cut -d@ -f2 > digest.txt
cat digest.txt
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel role=core-index
CMD ["echo", "CORE INDEX 1.0 READY"]

validation.description: The image `localhost:5000/kestrel/core-index:1.0` is present locally again
The local image is the `core-index` image from the depot (label `role=core-index`)
`/workspace/digest.txt` contains a `sha256:` digest

params.command: d=$(tr -d ' \r\n' < /workspace/digest.txt); r=$(curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/core-index/manifests/1.0 | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}'); [ -n "$r" ] && echo "$d" | grep -qF "$r" && echo digest-matches

validation.description: The digest in `digest.txt` equals the manifest digest the depot reports for `kestrel/core-index:1.0`

missions.debrief: Tags can move, but a digest names exactly one set of bytes, so recording it is how you prove a transfer was faithful. Pro tip: pull or run `name@sha256:...` to pin an image to that exact digest, whatever the tag does later.

missions.title: Sneakernet
missions.story:
Radio, channel 9. Wind noise, then Captain Rafael Duarte of the *Petrel*:

"Kestrel Point, the relay is dead again and I sail at dawn. I can carry files. Put the ice-report image on a tar in the outbox and I will take it to the mainland. In return I have a tar from the mainland team with their patch kit. It is in your inbox already. Over."

No registry, no network: move the images the old way, as files.
objectives: Save the local image `kestrel/ice-report:3.2` to the tar file `/workspace/outbox/ice-report.tar`
Load `/workspace/inbox/mainland-patchkit.tar` so that the image `mainland/patchkit:7` exists
missions.startingState: `/workspace/outbox/` is empty and `/workspace/inbox/mainland-patchkit.tar` has arrived. The image `kestrel/ice-report:3.2` is built locally; `mainland/patchkit:7` is not on this machine.
hints: Images can travel as plain files. One command writes an image and its layers into a tar archive, and its counterpart reads such an archive back into the local engine.

Use `docker save -o FILE.tar IMAGE:TAG` to export (do not gzip it) and `docker load -i FILE.tar` to import. Remember the outbox is `/workspace/outbox/` and the delivered tar sits in `/workspace/inbox/`.

```bash
docker save -o outbox/ice-report.tar kestrel/ice-report:3.2
docker load -i inbox/mainland-patchkit.tar
docker images mainland/patchkit
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel role=ice-report
CMD ["echo", "ICE REPORT 3.2"]

validation.description: `/workspace/outbox/ice-report.tar` exists
The outbox tar is a Docker image archive containing `kestrel/ice-report:3.2`
The image `mainland/patchkit:7` has been loaded
`mainland/patchkit:7` runs and prints `PATCHKIT 7`

missions.debrief: `docker save` and `docker load` turn images into ordinary files, which is how images cross an air gap on a ship, a USB stick or anything else. Pro tip: pass several image names to one `docker save` to bundle them, and they share layers inside the tar.

missions.title: Many Names, One Image
missions.story:
Kip's release checklist, copied from the whiteboard:

`[x] build kestrel/forecast:2.1.0`
`[ ] push 2.1.0`
`[ ] push 2.1, 2 and latest`
`[ ] tell Ingrid`

Amara spots the catch: the depot's `latest` still points at last week's 2.0.0, and every instrument host follows `latest`. Give the release all four names in the depot, 2.1.0, 2.1, 2 and latest, and make sure they are one and the same image.
objectives: Also publish it as `2.1`, `2` and `latest` under `localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast`
All four tags resolve to the same manifest digest in the depot
missions.startingState: The depot already holds `kestrel/forecast` with the tags `2.0.0` and `latest` (both the old release). The new `kestrel/forecast:2.1.0` exists only locally.
hints: A release usually carries several names: a full version, shorter version prefixes, and a moving `latest`. They are all just tags, so one image can wear them all, and re-pushing a tag moves it.

Give the local image one extra name per tag with `docker tag SOURCE localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:TAG`, then push each. Compare tags by asking the registry for each manifest's `Docker-Content-Digest` header.

```bash
for t in 2.1.0 2.1 2 latest; do
  docker tag kestrel/forecast:2.1.0 localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:$t
  docker push localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:$t
done
curl http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/tags/list
```

files.content:
FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel service=forecast version=2.0.0
CMD ["echo", "forecast 2.0.0"]

FROM alpine:3.20
LABEL station=kestrel service=forecast version=2.1.0
CMD ["echo", "forecast 2.1.0"]

validation.description: The depot lists the tags `2.1.0`, `2.1`, `2` and `latest` for `kestrel/forecast`

params.command: out=$(for t in 2.1.0 2.1 2 latest; do curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/manifests/$t | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}'; done); [ "$(echo "$out" | grep -c sha256)" = 4 ] && [ "$(echo "$out" | sort -u | wc -l)" = 1 ] && echo all-same

validation.description: All four tags (`2.1.0`, `2.1`, `2`, `latest`) have the same manifest digest in the depot

params.command: [ "$(curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/manifests/latest | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}')" != "$(curl -sI -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json, application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json, application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' http://localhost:5000/v2/kestrel/forecast/manifests/2.0.0 | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="docker-content-digest"{print $2}')" ] && echo moved

validation.description: `latest` no longer points at the old `2.0.0` release
The local image has the name `localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:latest`

solution: for t in 2.1.0 2.1 2 latest; do docker tag kestrel/forecast:2.1.0 localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:$t; docker push -q localhost:5000/kestrel/forecast:$t; done
missions.debrief: One image, four names: each push of an existing image only uploads a new tag, and every tag resolves to the same digest. `latest` is just a convention you have to move yourself. Pro tip: compare `Docker-Content-Digest` headers to prove that names really share one image.
